prerequisites: Knowledge of mathematics and physics content taught in the first year of respective degrees.

learning_outcomes.text: Identify and analyze the different components of electrical circuits and manage their analysis techniques.
Manage the analysis techniques of electrical circuits fed by sinusoidal sources.
Identify, analyze, and calculate balanced three-phase circuits and their application in industrial electrical installations.
Manage the procedures and measurement instruments for electrical circuits.
Describe and analyze the operating principle of electrical machines and their applications.

syllabus_topics: I. FUNDAMENTALS OF ELECTRICAL CIRCUITS: DC CIRCUITS
Fundamental electrical quantities and units
Electrical charges, electric current intensity, electric charge, electric voltage between two points and electromotive force, electric power, electric energy. Multiples and submultiples.
Sign conventions and graphical references
Electric charge, electric current intensity, electric voltage between two points and electromotive force, power and electric energy (generator and receiver criteria)
Fundamental concepts of electrical circuits:
Definition of electrical circuit
Introduction to active and passive elements of electrical circuits
Fundamental topological entities of electrical circuits: branch, node, loop, graph, planar circuit, mesh
Kirchhoff's Laws
Series and parallel connection of elements
Characteristic waveforms of electrical circuits
Transient and permanent regimes
Bidirectional and unidirectional waveforms
Periodic waveforms: period, cycle, frequency, phase shift between waves, peak values, peak-to-peak value, average value, RMS value
Components of electrical circuits

Ideal passive elements: the resistance (Ohm's Law, resistance (R), conductance, short circuit, open circuit, ideal switch, resistance of a conductor, resistivity and conductivity, instantaneous dissipated power, dissipated energy and Joule effect, real resistors, color code)
Ideal passive elements: the inductance (v-i behavior of inductance, self-inductance (L), charged inductance, instantaneous power absorbed by an inductance, energy stored by an inductance, real coils)
Ideal passive elements: magnetically coupled inductances

Ideal passive elements: the capacitance (v-i behavior of capacitance, capacitance (C), charged inductance, instantaneous power absorbed by a capacitance, energy stored by a capacitance, real capacitors)
Associations and equivalences of ideal passive elements: operational impedance and admittance (generalization of Ohm's Law), series association, parallel association, Kennelly's Theorem
Ideal active elements: ideal voltage sources, ideal current sources, series and parallel association of ideal voltage and current sources, ideal dependent sources
Real active elements: real voltage sources, real current sources, Maximum Power Transfer Theorem, equivalence between real voltage and current sources
Measurement elements: ideal ammeters and voltmeters
II. CIRCUITS IN SINUSOIDAL STEADY STATE
Sinusoidal waveforms: relevance, amplitude, angular frequency, phase angle, initial phase angle, particularization of characteristic parameters of periodic waves
Complex representation of sinusoidal waves: phasors
Complex impedance and admittance: generalization of Ohm's Law in complex notation
Systematic analysis of circuits in sinusoidal steady state in the complex domain
Response of R, L, C, RL and RC series dipoles in sinusoidal steady state: phasor diagram
Power and energy in sinusoidal steady state
Concepts of active, reactive and apparent power
Instantaneous power and energy, and active, reactive and apparent power in R, L, C, RL and RC series dipoles
Complex power
Power triangle
Boucherot's Theorem
Power factor: concept, relevance and correction
Introduction to frequency response of electrical circuits in sinusoidal steady state: series and parallel resonance
III. TOPOLOGICAL METHODS AND THEOREMS
Resolution of circuits using the mesh method
Resolution of circuits using the node method
Millman's Theorem
Superposition theorem
Thévenin's theorem
Generalization of the Maximum Power Transfer Theorem
Norton's theorem
IV. THREE-PHASE CIRCUITS
Generalities
Balanced and unbalanced three-phase voltage systems
Phase sequence
Balanced and unbalanced three-phase current loads and systems
Topologies of three-phase circuits
Four-wire star-star
Phase conductors and neutral wire
Three-wire star-star
Three-phase circuits with delta connections
Line and phase quantities, and their relationship
Star-delta and delta-star equivalences
Resolution of balanced three-phase circuits
Equivalent single-phase circuit
Power in three-phase circuits
Instantaneous power in three-phase elements
Active, reactive and apparent power in three-phase elements
Power triangle, complex power, Boucherot's Theorem, power factor
Correction of power factor in three-phase installations
Introduction to the generation, transmission, and distribution of electrical energy
V. ELECTRICAL MACHINES
Introduction to transformers
Introduction to asynchronous machines
Introduction to synchronous machines
PROGRAM OF LABORATORY PRACTICES:
P1: Description of equipment and assembly of DC circuits
P2: Assembly of circuits in sinusoidal steady state I
P3: Assembly of circuits in sinusoidal steady state II
P4: Exam
assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, if partial exam conditions are met (at least 20% per exercise and 50% global), the final grade is calculated as (0.4 * Partial Exam) + (0.15 * Laboratory Exam) + (0.45 * Final Exam); otherwise, or if the student opts to improve, it is (0.15 * Laboratory Exam) + (0.85 * Final Exam). In both ordinary cases, a minimum final grade of 5 points is required to pass, and failure to meet specific minimums (20% per exercise and 50% global in EP or EF) results in a maximum grade of 3.5 points. For extraordinary and differentiated calls, the final grade is always (0.15 * Laboratory Exam) + (0.85 * Final Exam). A minimum final grade of 5 points is needed to pass, and a maximum of 3.5 points is awarded if specific minimums in the Final Exam (20% per exercise and 50% global) are not achieved.
